content.thinking:
I'm piecing together the timeline: the monthly-spend-feature flag was switched on at 00:10:00Z, triggering ZeroDivisionError crashes in spend_summary.py:47 between 00:10 and 00:18, and I'm cross-referencing the flag evaluation counts (G971b off/on split and Gce95's 200 on-evaluations) to confirm the rollout coincided with the error spike.

Then at 00:17:03Z Argus switched the flag off, but Gce95 still shows it evaluating "on" through 00:18 — the revert never propagated to the service — and shortly after, M1 refuted the toggle and flag got set back to ON, meaning the harm kept going. I'm now building the causal chain: shoppers' account pages failed (Gbac1), those requests hit the ZeroDivisionError (G5309), and that happened because the service was still routing through the monthly spend summary path since the flag was evaluating "on" (G971b, Gce95).

I'm checking what else could explain the onset so I can rule those out — the deploy query only returned one earlier change (P1) via T8/T9, nothing new in the window, so a deploy isn't the cause, and prior to 00:10 the flag was off with healthy metrics (G7e5d, Gad41, Gbac1 near baseline), reinforcing that the flag flip is the real trigger.

Next I need to name the actual change: the admin turned on the monthly-spend-feature flag at P1, dated per P1.1, with no Argus action involved. Then I trace why that broke things — the flag routes shoppers to a function computing average spend per item this month, dividing total by purchase count this month, which is zero for shoppers with prior purchases but none this month, causing a ZeroDivisionError (F1). So the final step in the chain states plainly that enabling the flag routed those shoppers into a calculation that fails for them, citing F1 and G5309, leaving the deeper mechanism for the root cause section.

Ordering the chain: symptom first, then the ZeroDivisionError at line 47, then the explanation that the flag was switched on (citing P1, G971b, G971b, Gce95, with alternatives ruled out), then the explanation of why that broke things (F1). I'm checking that step three correctly dates the change using P1.1 and reads state by row instant, and confirming Gce95 shows the flag on through 00:18, which checks out.

For the root-cause justification, I note that the mechanism — division failing on an empty count — rests on F1, and G5309 is the log evidence showing the ZeroDivisionError at line 47. The detail about it affecting shoppers with no purchases this month also rests on F1, and I don't see any S or D row contradicting that, so it holds. I conclude the chain does reach a genuine cause.

Now I'm drafting the root-cause statement itself: the spend-summary function divides total spend by purchase count without guarding against zero purchases, so shoppers who've bought before but not this month trigger a ZeroDivisionError at line 47, and with the monthly-spend-feature flag on, the summary renderer calls this function for exactly those shoppers' account pages, causing the failure. I'm deciding how to cite the line number as a figure/label without miscategorizing it, settling on referencing it as the line the log names. Then I start listing contributing factors, beginning with the absence of any check that would have caught the division issue.

For CF-2, the flag flipped from 129 off/71 on to fully on in a single minute with no staged rollout visible — a percentage-based rollout with automatic halt on rising errors would have limited the blast radius. I'd propose gating flag enablement on progressive rollout with error-triggered halts, and that safeguard would have held before.

For CF-3, nobody was paged since the alert didn't link to an on-call incident — had someone been on call, they could have investigated why the revert wasn't reaching the service sooner and escalated faster.

Now I'm checking CF-4: the flag switch-off didn't reach the service, since logs show "monthly-spend-feature=on" at 00:11–00:18 even though Argus switched it off at 00:17:03. That propagation gap is a system condition, not a response factor, and fixing it would have ended the harm sooner.

Though why_it_did_not_help covers this as investigation rather than an action item, so rather than duplicate it as a separate CF, I'll fold the mis-propagation detail into went_wrong instead.

Since the switch-off was judged refuted, the flag got put back ON, leaving the failing path in place and the harm ongoing — that's another went_wrong item. There's a minor timestamp conflict between C2 and P2 on when Argus switched off, but I'll skip that as inconsequential. For stops_the_harm, I need the switch-off to actually take effect at the service level, confirmed through its logs showing the flag evaluating off and the ZeroDiv issue resolved.

For why_it_did_not_help, the key question is whether the switch-off reached io-shop at all — the logs still showed it evaluating on afterward — and if it did reach, why pages kept failing anyway. For still_at_risk, I want to stick strictly to what the record supports: accounts could keep failing while the flag stays on, without overstating what a future attempt would do.

For action items, I'm separating prevention measures into distinct, single-purpose items — one requiring CI to test flag-gated paths both on and off before production enablement, and another for progressive rollout with automatic halt on error spikes, which I should probably split further since each is really its own fix.

For process improvement, routing HighErrorRate alerts on io-shop to an on-call rota addresses CF-3. I'm ruling out deploy as a cause since the change query during onset only turned up the flag change, with all replicas on one revision, so there's no deploy-related factor worth including.

I'm also ruling out client disconnects, since those errors (G46bc, Gbac1, Gad41) ran before onset while the service was healthy, not caused by the incident.

What went well: the Investigator Agent correctly placed onset at the minute the flag was switched on, and tied the errors to the monthly-spend-feature and the ZeroDivision issue.

For mitigation, the agent verified the service after flipping the flag off rather than assuming success, found it still at incident-level severity, and then proposed a draft PR as a code fix. I don't see anything that looks like pure luck here — G971b's transitional evaluation count at 00:10 doesn't really qualify. Key assumption to flag: the failing shoppers are being defined as those with no purchases this month, per Code-Fix's interpretation.

I'm framing the cause in plain terms — switching on a new monthly spending feature routed account pages through a calculation that divides by this month's purchase count, crashing for shoppers who've bought before but not this month. The symptom is simply that shoppers' account pages failed, and none of the three contributing factors have anything addressing them yet.

Now I'm mapping each step's citations: step 1 to the admin's switch-on and error-rate alert, step 2 to the error-rate range, step 3 to the feature being switched on and the logged evaluations turning on and running through a specific time range, and step 4 to the code line and error-rate data. I want to make sure each timestamp and range reference lines up correctly with its source.

action_items.item: Make CI run io-shop's test suite with each feature flag switched on, as well as off, before that flag can be enabled in production.
Enable feature flags on io-shop in percentage steps rather than for all traffic at once.
Automatically halt and roll back a flag rollout step on io-shop when the error rate rises above its baseline.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call rota so that it pages a person.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed, and the service logged the account page error rate climbing over the last minute.
Those requests raised ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py line {F1.1}, logged throughout {G5309.3} and not before the onset.

ruled_out.what: A deployment: the query for production changes over the day before the onset found only the flag change, and the rollout read showed every replica on one revision
Shoppers closing their connections: those errors were logged while the service was healthy before the onset, with the account page error rate at its usual level, and they stopped at the onset

causal_chain.step: The service was taking the code path that raises the error because admin switched the feature flag monthly-spend-feature on at {P1.1}. The service logged its evaluations of the flag turning on at {G971b.6} and logged them all on over {Gce95.4}. Before that, the flag evaluated off over {G7e5d.4}, and account pages rendered normally.
Turning the flag on sent the account pages of shoppers with no purchases this month into a calculation that divides by zero for them.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Turning on a new monthly-spending feature sent shoppers' account pages through a calculation that crashes, most likely for shoppers who have bought before but not this month, because it divides by the number of purchases they made this month.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that ran the account page with monthly-spend-feature on for an account with no purchases this month before the flag was switched on in production. Code-Fix's reading says the existing tests do not cover this case.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The division by zero would have failed a test before the flag reached shoppers, and the flag would not have been switched on with the fault in place.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from off to on for all of the service's traffic within the onset minute. No staged rollout and no automatic halt on rising errors were seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A small share of shoppers would have hit the failure first, and the rollout could have stopped before most account pages failed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was linked to no on-call incident, so nobody was paged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been on the incident when switching the flag off did not show at the service, and could have chased why the service still evaluated it on, rather than the incident going to escalation with the harm still going on.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent placed the onset at the minute the flag was switched on.
The Investigator Agent formed a candidate that tied the errors to monthly-spend-feature and to the failing line named in the logs.
The Mitigation Agent took an action that could be put back, then looked at the service instead of assuming the action worked, and found it still at the incident's level.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request PR #414 for a person to review.

went_wrong: Switching monthly-spend-feature off at the provider did not show at the service: its logs still recorded the flag evaluating on through the minute after the switch-off, and account page requests kept failing.
Rather than finding why the switch-off had not shown at the service, the second investigation came back with the same flag explanation, so Argus had nothing left to try while the harm went on.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, `render_spend_summary` calls `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. That function divides the account's spend this month by the number of purchases made this month and does not handle an empty list, so for a shopper who has bought before but not this month it raises ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1}, and `serve_account_page` fails that shopper's account page.
input.still_at_risk: With monthly-spend-feature left on, shoppers' account pages could keep failing with division-by-zero errors.
input.stops_the_harm: Switch monthly-spend-feature off at whatever io-shop actually reads its flag decision from. Confirm at the service that its logs record the flag evaluating off and that the ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py stops being logged.
input.why_it_did_not_help: Find out whether the switch-off of monthly-spend-feature at the provider ever reached io-shop, given that the service's logs still recorded the flag evaluating on afterwards. If it did reach the service, find out why account pages kept failing.
